items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: I have two John Williams in, he’s great, I love John Williams, “Star Wars” and “Can You Read My Mind,”

ctx.x: Yeah, talking about the process of recording music, I mean you’ve seen from your days with Bunny Berigan up until your most recent one hundredth album, which I wanted to mention, you’ve seen a great deal of change in the actual technology of recording. Do you think it’s affected the music in the way it’s written, the way that technology has changed the recording of it?

It has in this way, that well let’s see, it’s hard to answer that. You know I think overdubbing has changed things a little bit. Because I remember as long as I’ve been in this business you’re always learning new things. The very last album I did was this one here called “I Love Movies” which is a very new album. It just reached the market, and it’s movie themes, stuff like “Star Wars,” John Williams — I have two John Williams in, he’s great, I love John Williams, “Star Wars” and “Can You Read My Mind,” — talk…

Nice.” You don’t get brass leaking into singers, like we have on “S’ Wonderful.” You don’t get brass leaking into piano, and drums leaking into piano. And you get clean tracks on everybody. But you do lose something I think. You lose the idea of 28 people in the studio at the same time recording a piece of music and hearing what everybody else is doing, and how the finished product is sounding. With the brass overdubbing technique, you do your rhythm tracks and the drummers are hearing the guitars on earphones.…
